paras: The attempted lynching of Hicks Carmichael took place at Knoxville, Tennessee, on the night of May 24, 1888, when a crowd of about 2,000 men and boys gathered at the jail demanding Carmichael, a Black laborer charged with killing Knox County Deputy Sheriff D. A. Shipe four days earlier. Officers had already removed him, and he spent the night in the jail at Chattanooga. Brought back under armed guard, he was tried and sentenced on May 26 and hanged in the Knoxville jail on July 20. Papers disagreed over whether any lynching had been attempted, and Knoxville dispatches later called the early reports exaggerated.

On Sunday morning, May 20, Shipe went with a warrant to a laborer's tent on the new railroad works near Flat Creek church, fifteen to twenty miles north of Knoxville, taking Constable W. A. Coram with him. The first wire named the man as "Hicks Martin, a negro," wanted in Alabama for murder, and a fuller dispatch added a robbery charge in Morgan County.

According to the dispatches, the man fired two revolvers as the officers came to the tent, killing Shipe in the doorway and putting a bullet through Coram's coat. He fled while officers and citizens gave chase, and the first wire predicted that if taken alive "he will be lynched."

On the night of May 23 an officer fired a load of buckshot into him, but he escaped in the dark by swimming a river. The next morning a dozen men surrounded him near Rankin's Depot in Cocke County, by one account in a barn. He reached Knoxville by train at about noon, and a crowd the Memphis Appeal put at 1,000 and the Savannah Morning News at 2,000 followed him to the jail.

A dispatch printed in the Somerset Herald said an "angry mob" surrounded the jail threatening to take him out, while the chief of police and his captors urged it to let the law take its course. At about eight o'clock, the Appeal's correspondent wrote, 2,000 or more men and boys massed at the jail, yelling for the prisoner, until the sheriff and jailor let them search it. Carmichael was gone: a Chattanooga dispatch said he had been brought to the Hamilton County jail that night "to save a lynching at Knoxville."

Indicted on May 24, Carmichael was returned at 2 a.m. on May 26 and met at the depot by police and twenty armed men. That morning, before Judge Logan and with Gen. R. N. Hood appointed as counsel, a jury found him guilty of first-degree murder. He was sentenced to hang on July 20, while thirty citizens with shotguns and the Knoxville Rifles stood guard. The judge ordered the arrest of those in the Thursday night demonstration, though no report of their prosecution appears in the coverage.
Sheriff Jones hanged Carmichael inside the jail on July 20 before relatives of both men, and his body was to be buried in Cocke County, where his mother lived.

White papers carried the episode mainly as Knoxville wire copy, from the New York Sun and the Memphis Appeal to the Wilmington Daily Republican. Their language centered on race and guilt, as in the Macon Beacon's headline "A White Deputy Sheriff Shot Down By a Colored Man" and the Somerset Herald's "Thirsting for His Blood." News digests in Ohio and Kentucky reported only that "Citizens of Knoxville threaten to lynch Hicks Carmichael."

The Memphis Appeal first headed its special "A Disgraceful Mob" and called the crowd "wild animals," but after the trial dismissed it as "loafing drunken boys" under the headline "He Will Hang." The conviction wire, run in Atlanta, Savannah and Richmond, added that "Exaggerated accounts of attempts to lynch Carmichael have been telegraphed from Knoxville," and the Johnson City Comet said Nashville American reports were "greatly exaggerated."

The capture wire stated that "No attempt was made to lynch Carmichael," though it does not mention the night crowd, and the Comet found "no disposition whatever to lynch the negro." Against these, the Appeal's July retrospective said threats were "freely made, and an attempt to carry them out was made that night." That account also dated the trial "May 6," an evident error for the May 26 given in contemporary reports.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Hicks Carmichael
bases: A crowd of 1,000 to 2,000 surrounded and searched the Knoxville jail for a prisoner charged with killing a deputy, threatening to take him out, after officers had removed him (A7, A15, A14); he was later legally tried and hanged (A16, A23).
The jail crowd acted without authority and in large numbers to punish an accused killer (A7, A15), but it never reached him; he was killed only by legal execution after a trial (A16, A20, A23).
Several dispatches describe a mob threatening and searching the jail (A7, A15, A21), but others say no attempt was made and that lynching reports were exaggerated (A5, A13, A16).

accounts.gist: A 'howling mob' of 2,000 or more men and boys gathered at the jail at night and was allowed to search it; officers had spirited the prisoner away.

accounts.label: Somerset Herald dispatch (May 24)
accounts.gist: An angry mob surrounded the jail threatening to take him out despite appeals from the police chief and his captors; signs of an attempt at 10 o'clock.

accounts.label: Capture wire (May 24)
accounts.gist: A crowd of 2,000 followed him to jail, but no attempt was made to lynch him.

accounts.label: Knoxville wire and Comet (May 26)
accounts.gist: Accounts of lynching attempts were exaggerated and there was no danger or disposition to lynch.

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal execution account (July 20)
accounts.gist: Threats of lynching were made and an attempt was made that night, forcing removal to Chattanooga.

framing.detail: Memphis Appeal headlined 'A Disgraceful Mob' and called the crowd 'wild animals', later dismissing it as 'loafing drunken boys' and praising the quick trial ('He Will Hang').
Most papers ran Knoxville wires calling him 'the negro who murdered' Shipe and reporting the conviction, with the line that lynching accounts were 'exaggerated'.
Somerset Herald's 'Thirsting for His Blood' called him 'the most desperate negro in East Tennessee' and doubted the trial promise would save 'the doomed man'.
The first wire predicted he would be lynched if taken alive; the Macon Beacon headlined 'A White Deputy Sheriff Shot Down By a Colored Man'.
